The search turned up no official OpenAI Agents SDK long-term memory feature. The SDK's built-in sessions handle short-term conversation history, and the long-term layer comes from a third-party package.

- **Built-in sessions:** The official docs describe sessions as storing conversation history for a specific session. SQLiteSession takes a session ID and an optional database file, and different session IDs maintain separate conversation histories.
- **Compaction:** The docs also list an OpenAIResponsesCompactionSession, which compacts stored history using the Responses API. This is still history management, not persistent memory across users.
- **Third-party long-term memory:** The mem01session package adds cross-conversation memory. It keeps the exact short-term item chain in the SDK's SQLiteSession, while the embedded mem01 engine extracts and recalls long-term beliefs through OpenAI and Postgres/pgvector. Its v0.1.1 listing says the DATABASE_URL setting is required, and items are partitioned by session_id.
- **Management APIs:** The package exposes memory_history(), correct_memory(), and forget_memory() for managing stored beliefs, and memory is failure-open by default, so raw SQLite persistence still succeeds if memory extraction fails.

Caveat: these results are mostly the package's own PyPI pages, and I found no independent review of it. I also didn't find any 2026 announcement from OpenAI about native long-term memory in the SDK, so that is worth checking against the official changelog.

Honest limits, and what would fill each one:

| Gap | Risk | What would fill it |
|---|---|---|
| **Memory poisoning / prompt injection** (OWASP's 2026 Top 10 for agentic applications lists it as ASI06, memory and context poisoning) | Text the user (or a pasted document) says is stored, then returned in future prompts as trusted memory, and it outlives the session | Store provenance and source type; treat memory as data in the prompt; filter instruction-like text at write time; review high-impact memories |

| **Keyword retrieval** | Rare exact words missed by embeddings | Full-text index + rank fusion (D11) |
| **Reflection / insights** | No higher-level conclusions ("Alex is happier since moving") | Scheduled LLM reflection writing new `insight` memories with evidence links |
| **Procedural memory learning** | The companion doesn't learn *how* to talk to this person beyond boundaries | Store style feedback as memories that edit the persona prompt; review before applying |
| **Multimodal memory** | Photos, voice, documents | Embeddings for images/audio, `Media` nodes linked `ABOUT` entities |
| **Shared memory across people** | Two users who know the same Maya have two Mayas | Global entity layer with consent; cross-user resolution |
| **Erasure outside the graph** | Backups, logs, traces, LLM provider retention | Retention policies, log redaction, provider no-retention settings |

| **Benchmarks** | Our scenarios aren't comparable with other systems | Run LoCoMo / LongMemEval / BEAM-style suites |
| **Learned thresholds** | Hand-measured cut-offs per model | Collect labelled pairs from the trace UI and refit |
| **Non-English** | Role-name rules and regexes are English | Language-aware rules; multilingual embedding model (Qwen3 is multilingual) |

The same term often has a precise academic meaning, a working meaning among practitioners,
and a looser one in product marketing ("marketecture"). None is wrong, but mixing them causes
most design arguments. The last column says where this repo stands.

| Term | Academic / standards meaning | Practitioner meaning | Loose / marketing meaning | This repo |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Agent memory** | Long-term stores an agent reads and writes during its decision cycle (CoALA) | Persisting facts about users across sessions, plus retrieval into the prompt | Any feature that makes a chatbot "remember you"; "infinite memory", "perfect recall" | The practitioner meaning, with the psychology kinds made explicit (Lesson 8) |
| **Memory layer** | — (not an academic term) | A service between the app and the LLM that extracts, stores and retrieves memories (Mem0, Zep) | "Add memory to any agent in 3 lines" | A library-sized memory layer you can read end to end (`MemoryStore`) |
| **Context engineering** | Generalizes "context" from HCI (Dey); framed in 2025 papers as assembling the model's input | Choosing which tokens go into each call: instructions, tools, retrieved data, memory, history. The term spread in mid-2025 (Cognition, Shopify's CEO, Anthropic's September 2025 guide) | A rebrand of prompt engineering | `recall()` + `format_context()` + the trace that shows the result (Lessons 10, 18) |
| **Knowledge graph** | Entities and typed relations, usually under an ontology, often with reasoning (KR, Semantic Web) | A property graph of entities and facts used for search or RAG | Any graph database, or any data with links | Life graph + memories + RelType ontology ([knowledge graph](#knowledge-graph)) |
| **Temporal / bi-temporal KG** | Facts with valid time, and with transaction time too (temporal databases) | Facts that expire or get superseded instead of overwritten (Graphiti) | "Memory that understands time" | Bi-temporal memories and relations (Lessons 8, 13) |
| **Context graph** | — (a 2025–26 industry term) | A graph of *decisions*: policies, exceptions, precedents, evidence and outcomes, so agents know *why* something happened. Thoughtworks' Radar (April 2026) rates it "Assess" | The next thing after knowledge graphs | Partly: provenance (`FROM` episode), supersession history and the trace record what was *said* and *decided by the code*, but not decisions with reasons as nodes |
| **Ontology** | OWL/RDFS classes, properties and axioms with formal semantics | A typed vocabulary with rules shared by a team | Palantir's *Ontology*: an operational layer of business objects, links **and actions** that apps and agents act through; or any data model | A lightweight ontology (sense 2 under [ontology](#ontology)), no actions |
| **Semantic layer** | — (BI and data-warehouse term) | Governed definitions of metrics and dimensions over a warehouse (dbt, Snowflake semantic models, LookML) | "The semantic layer for AI": any metadata an agent can read | Not used. The ontology plays the "agreed meaning" role for relation types |
| **GraphRAG** | Microsoft Research's method (2024): an entity graph plus community summaries for global questions; later DRIFT and LazyGraphRAG | Any RAG that retrieves through a graph, usually vector entry points + traversal | "RAG, but with a graph, so no hallucinations" | The local style (Lessons 5, 10) |
| **Hybrid search** | Lexical (BM25) + dense retrieval, fused (e.g. reciprocal-rank fusion) | Same, or vector + graph | "Best of both worlds" | Vector + graph; no lexical retriever yet ([D11](design-decisions.md#d11)) |
| **Vector database** | — | A database built around ANN indexes (Pinecone, Qdrant, Milvus...) | Anything with a vector index, including general databases | A vector index inside Neo4j ([D1](design-decisions.md#d1)) |
| **Agentic RAG** | — | The model decides when and what to retrieve, in a loop, through tools | Any RAG with an LLM involved | Lesson 7 is agentic; the companion's recall is not ([D10](design-decisions.md#d10)) |
| **Reranking** | Re-scoring a candidate list with a stronger model (cross-encoder, learning to rank) | Same, often a hosted reranker API | — | A formula plus an optional cross-encoder label ([rerank and relevance](#rerank-and-relevance)) |
| **Consolidation / sleep-time compute** | Memory consolidation in neuroscience (sleep strengthens and reorganizes memories) | Background jobs that rewrite memory between conversations (Letta's sleep-time agents) | "Your agent learns while it sleeps" | End-of-episode pass + `consolidate()` (Lessons 11, 13) |
| **Memory poisoning** | Data poisoning / prompt injection research applied to stored memory | Malicious or mistaken text stored as memory and trusted later; ASI06 in OWASP's 2026 Top 10 for agentic applications | — | A known gap ([gaps](design-decisions.md#gaps-what-this-design-does-not-cover)) |
| **Long-term memory benchmark** | Datasets with defined tasks: LoCoMo (2024), LongMemEval (2024: adds knowledge updates and abstention), BEAM (2026: 1M–10M tokens) | Leaderboard numbers on those | Self-reported scores across vendors, often with different settings | Not run; our scenarios are code-graded and repo-specific ([D20](design-decisions.md#d20)) |
| **Digital twin** | A simulation model kept in sync with a physical system | A live model of an organization's entities and processes | Any database about real things | Not used |

**How to read a vendor claim:**
1. Ask which **sense** of the word is meant, using the table above.
Only (1) and (4) remove data.

### instruction

(1) a **system prompt** or persona instruction to the chat model; (2) an embedding model's
**query instruction**: text put before a query so the model embeds it for retrieval
(Lesson 19); (3) instruction-tuned models in general. Sense 2 is never seen by the chat model.

"""Lesson 19 — the companion's embedding model: where it runs, and the thresholds measured for it.

Every similarity cut-off in the memory store (is this a duplicate? the same person? part of a
habit?) was measured on ONE model's scores. Another model spreads its scores differently, so
switching models without re-measuring silently breaks dedupe, entity matching and recall.
A Profile keeps a model and its thresholds together:

    local   BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5    384 dims, on the CPU via fastembed, no key   (default)
    remote  Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-8B   4096 dims, any OpenAI-compatible /embeddings endpoint

Each model's vectors live in their own property and vector indexes ("embedding" + memory_vec
for the default, "embedding_qwen3_embedding_8b" + memory_vec_qwen3_embedding_8b for Qwen), so
one database can hold both: the tests run on the local model while your chats use the remote
one, and `python -m companion.reembed` backfills a model's vectors after a switch.

Queries vs passages: Qwen3-Embedding is trained to put an instruction before a QUERY ("what
does this message relate to?") and nothing before a stored text. Without it, its separation
of related from unrelated memories fell from 0.99 to 0.90 AUC (lessons/19). So `embed(...,
query=True)` is for a message searched against memories; comparisons between two stored
things (memory vs memory, entity vs entity) use plain embeddings on both sides.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import re
import threading
from collections import OrderedDict
from dataclasses import dataclass

import numpy as np

import config


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Profile:
    model: str
    dims: int
    # Thresholds. "score" = the vector index's 0-1 score, (1 + cosine) / 2; "cosine" = raw.
    duplicate: float          # score: a new memory this close to a current one reinforces it
    forgotten: float          # cosine: this close to a /forget tombstone is not stored again
    entity_match: float       # score: an entity this close (same kind) may be the same one...
    name_match: float         # cosine: ...if their NAMES are this close too ("Mom" ~ "my mother")
    pattern: float            # cosine: every pair in a habit cluster at least this close
    sensitive_floor: float    # score: a sensitive memory needs at least this to be recalled
    sensitive_margin: float   # score: ...and to be within this of the best match
    entity_hop: float         # score: an entity this close to the message is looked up
    query_instruction: str = ""    # put before a query (not before stored text)
    cluster_instruction: str = ""  # put before memories grouped into habits (Lesson 13)
    # score: below this a vector match is "loosely related" (Lesson 18). None: the model can't
    # tell (bge-small's scores overlap), so a cross-encoder decides instead.
    weak_below: float | None = None

    @property
    def slug(self) -> str:
        """'' for the default model (the property and index names from Lessons 8-18)."""
        if self.model == DEFAULT_MODEL:
            return ""
        return re.sub(r"[^a-z0-9]+", "_", self.model.split("/")[-1].lower()).strip("_")

    @property
    def prop(self) -> str:
        return f"embedding_{self.slug}" if self.slug else "embedding"

    def index(self, base: str) -> str:
        return f"{base}_{self.slug}" if self.slug else base


DEFAULT_MODEL = config.LOCAL_EMBED_MODEL

PROFILES = {p.model: p for p in [
    # Lessons 9-13 measured these (see the comments next to each constant in store.py).
    Profile("BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5", dims=384, duplicate=0.975, forgotten=0.90, entity_match=0.93,
            name_match=0.80, pattern=0.82, sensitive_floor=0.72, sensitive_margin=0.01, entity_hop=0.85),
    # Lesson 19: measured with `python -m companion.calibrate` (results in the lesson).
    # Its scores spread wider than bge-small's: unrelated pairs sit lower (sensitive/hop "no"
    # 0.57-0.62 vs bge's 0.68-0.74), so the floors drop, and a message that only MEANS an
    # entity ("how is my kid doing?" -> Logan) now clears the hop (0.65-0.73 vs no <= 0.59).
    Profile("Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-8B", dims=4096, duplicate=0.966, forgotten=0.89, entity_match=0.94,
            name_match=0.84, pattern=0.665, sensitive_floor=0.655, sensitive_margin=0.015, entity_hop=0.62,
            query_instruction="Instruct: Given a message from a user, retrieve memories about the "
                              "user's life that it relates to\nQuery: ",
            # without it, "heading to the gym" vs "went rock climbing" (0.77) outscored two
            # gym sentences (0.73): complete-linkage clustering couldn't find the habit
            cluster_instruction="Instruct: Identify the activity or habit described\nQuery: ",
            # one cut on the best match got 36 of 37 test messages right (raw cosine 0.312)
            weak_below=0.656),
]}


def profile_for(model: str) -> Profile:
    if model not in PROFILES:
        raise SystemExit(
            f"No thresholds measured for EMBED_MODEL={model!r}. Add a Profile for it in "
            "companion/embeddings.py, measured with `python -m companion.calibrate` (Lesson 19).")
    return PROFILES[model]


PROFILE = profile_for(config.EMBED_MODEL)

_local = None
_client = None
_lock = threading.Lock()
_cache: OrderedDict[tuple[str, str], np.ndarray] = OrderedDict()  # (instruction, text) -> unit vector
CACHE_SIZE = 2048  # names and summaries are embedded again and again during one extraction


def remote() -> bool:
    return bool(config.EMBED_BASE_URL)


def _compute(texts: list[str]) -> np.ndarray:
    global _local, _client
    if not remote():
        if _local is None:
            from fastembed import TextEmbedding
            _local = TextEmbedding(PROFILE.model)
        return np.array(list(_local.embed(texts)), dtype=np.float32)
    if _client is None:
        from openai import OpenAI
        _client = OpenAI(base_url=config.EMBED_BASE_URL, api_key=REDACTED, timeout=60, max_retries=3)
    out = []
    for i in range(0, len(texts), 64):  # endpoints cap the batch size
        resp = _client.embeddings.create(model=PROFILE.model, input=texts[i:i + 64], encoding_format="float")
        out += [d.embedding for d in sorted(resp.data, key=lambda d: d.index)]
    vecs = np.array(out, dtype=np.float32)
    if vecs.shape[1] != PROFILE.dims:
        raise RuntimeError(f"{PROFILE.model} returned {vecs.shape[1]} dims, expected {PROFILE.dims}")
    return vecs


def embed(texts: list[str], query: bool = False) -> list[list[float]]:
    """Unit-length vectors (so a dot product is the cosine). `query=True`: the text is a message
    searched against stored memories/entities, and gets the model's query instruction."""
    return _embed(texts, PROFILE.query_instruction if query else "")


def embed_for_clustering(texts: list[str]) -> list[list[float]]:
    """Vectors for grouping memories into habits. Not stored: consolidation embeds again
    when the model has a clustering instruction, else it can use the stored vectors."""
    return _embed(texts, PROFILE.cluster_instruction)


def _embed(texts: list[str], instruction: str) -> list[list[float]]:
    keys = [(instruction, t) for t in texts]
    found: dict[tuple[str, str], np.ndarray] = {}
    with _lock:
        for k in keys:
            if k in _cache:
                found[k] = _cache[k]
                _cache.move_to_end(k)
    missing = [k for k in dict.fromkeys(keys) if k not in found]
    if missing:
        vecs = _compute([i + t for i, t in missing])
        vecs /= np.linalg.norm(vecs, axis=1, keepdims=True)
        found.update(zip(missing, vecs))
        with _lock:
            _cache.update(zip(missing, vecs))
            while len(_cache) > CACHE_SIZE:
                _cache.popitem(last=False)
    return [found[k].tolist() for k in keys]
"""Lesson 19 — give every stored memory, entity and episode a vector from the active model.

    python -m companion.reembed              nodes that don't have one yet (after a switch)
    python -m companion.reembed --all        recompute every vector (e.g. a changed instruction)
    python -m companion.reembed --user Mark  one user only

Run it after changing EMBED_MODEL / EMBED_BASE_URL. Each model writes its own property
(embedding / embedding_<model>), so the old vectors stay and switching back costs nothing.
The text embedded is the same text the write path embeds (keep them in step: a vector made
from different text matches differently). Tombstones (:Forgotten) keep no text, so they
can't be re-embedded; they only matter while their episode is open, so that's harmless.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import sys
import time

from neo4j import GraphDatabase

from config import NEO4J_AUTH, NEO4J_URI
from companion.embeddings import PROFILE, embed, remote
from companion.schema import ensure_schema

# label -> Cypher for the text the write path embeds for it (store.py)
TEXTS = {
    "User": "n.name + ', the user'",
    "Entity": "n.name + ' (' + n.kind + '): ' + coalesce(n.summary, '')",
    "Memory": "n.text",
    "Episode": "n.summary",
}
BATCH = 64


def reembed(driver, user: str | None = None, everything: bool = False) -> dict[str, int]:
    """`user`: a user's name ("Mark"), as MemoryStore takes it; None for everyone."""
    user = f"user:{user.lower()}" if user else None  # the id MemoryStore gives that user
    ensure_schema(driver)  # this model's vector indexes
    counts = {}
    for label, text in TEXTS.items():
        where = ["n[$prop] IS NULL"] if not everything else []
        where += [f"{text} IS NOT NULL"]
        if label == "Entity":
            where.append("NOT n:User")
        if user:
            where.append("n.user = $user")
        rows, _, _ = driver.execute_query(
            f"MATCH (n:{label}) WHERE {' AND '.join(where)} RETURN elementId(n) AS id, {text} AS text",
            prop=PROFILE.prop, user=user)
        for i in range(0, len(rows), BATCH):
            chunk = rows[i:i + BATCH]
            vecs = embed([r["text"] for r in chunk])
            driver.execute_query(
                """
                UNWIND $rows AS row MATCH (n) WHERE elementId(n) = row.id
                CALL db.create.setNodeVectorProperty(n, $prop, row.vec)
                """,
                rows=[{"id": r["id"], "vec": v} for r, v in zip(chunk, vecs)], prop=PROFILE.prop)
        counts[label] = len(rows)
    return counts


def main() -> None:
    args = sys.argv[1:]
    user = args[args.index("--user") + 1] if "--user" in args else None
    where = f"{PROFILE.model} via {'the endpoint in EMBED_BASE_URL' if remote() else 'fastembed (local)'}"
    print(f"Embedding with {where} -> property {PROFILE.prop}")
    start = time.time()
    with GraphDatabase.driver(NEO4J_URI, auth=NEO4J_AUTH) as driver:
        counts = reembed(driver, user, everything="--all" in args)
    print(", ".join(f"{n} {label.lower()}" for label, n in counts.items()), f"in {time.time() - start:.1f}s")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

content.text:
I finished the fact-check, the code and design review, and the lesson-flow review, and verified the links. All 197 tests pass (the 42 that need a live LLM weren't run). Nothing is committed.

**Fact-check: the alternatives are now current to November 2026**
- **Design decisions, D1 alternatives:** I added three options:
  - **Other graph databases:** Memgraph, FalkorDB, Neptune, and LadybugDB for embedded use. Kuzu was archived in October 2025, and LadybugDB is its maintained fork.
  - **Cloud memory services:** Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory and Vertex AI Memory Bank.
  - **Memory kept as files:** Anthropic's memory tool and Letta's git-backed file memory, MemFS.
- **"How other memory systems choose":** new rows for Cognee, Neo4j Labs' `neo4j-agent-memory`, the cloud services, and file-based memory. The Letta row now mentions MemFS. A short note says where the field is heading: cloud services and file-based memory both leave out the graph.
- **Gaps:** added "reasoning memory", meaning stored traces of the agent's own decisions. Neo4j Labs' package has this and our design doesn't.
- **Glossary:** three new terms (reasoning memory, cloud memory bank, memory as files) and nine new sources.
- **Lesson 9:** the Mem0 row was out of date. It now says the LLM picks ADD/UPDATE/DELETE in Mem0 1.x, while Mem0 2.0 only adds and resolves conflicts when reading.
- **Lesson 7:** now mentions LangChain 1.0's `create_agent` and the Postgres checkpointer.
- **README and Lesson 8:** their lists of alternatives match the design doc.

**Code review**
I ran a linter and read the recently changed code.
- **Fixed in `companion/embeddings.py`:**
  - The local model or API client could be created twice when the background extractor and the chat started at the same moment. Creation now happens under a lock.
  - An all-zero vector caused a divide-by-zero. It is now guarded.
- **Fixed in the tests:** an unused import in `tests/test_19_embeddings.py`.
- **Left as they are:**
  - The broad `except Exception` blocks are deliberate fallbacks so memory extraction never breaks the chat.
  - The loop-variable lambda in consolidation runs immediately, so it's safe.
  - The web page escapes every piece of text it inserts, and the server listens only on 127.0.0.1.

**Educational flow and links**
- Lessons 0–5 and 7–9 had no "Next" section, and Lesson 10's list stopped at Lesson 17. Every lesson now ends with a "## Next" section that leads into the next lesson's story.
- Every lesson also ends with a bar linking the previous lesson, all lessons, and the next lesson.
- Lesson 10 got an opening line linking it to Lesson 9, and the titles of Lessons 18–19 now match the others.
- All 471 internal links and anchors resolve.
- All external URLs load except three API base URLs (a 404 is normal for those) and Microsoft Research, which blocks automated checks.

input.ask: Make the tests model-aware and recommend remote for the companion?

content.text:
No, I wouldn't require remote embeddings everywhere, but the companion should use the larger model by default. And the tests aren't fully up to date: most of them assume the small local model, and 10 fail on Qwen.

**What I measured.** I ran the full suite against Qwen3-Embedding-8B. 187 of 197 tests pass, compared with 197 of 197 on the small local model, bge-small. The 10 failures:

- **Nine assume bge-small.** They hard-code its numbers or behaviour:
  - the 0.975 duplicate cut-off (`test_18` ×2);
  - the cross-encoder's relevance labels (`test_10` ×2, `test_19` weak labels);
  - the local calibration pairs and the default `embedding` property name (`test_19` ×3);
  - one clustering test (`test_13`), where Qwen puts a fourth gym sentence in the group.
  
  None of these show a problem in Qwen's results. The tests just don't account for the model.
- **One is a real quality difference.** Qwen scores "Bob" vs "Robert" at 0.837, just under its 0.84 name-match cut-off, so "Bob" isn't kept as an alias. Lesson 19 already calls this a tradeoff: Qwen gets 10 of 13 name pairs right, and nicknames usually come from the extractor anyway.
- **The LLM evals run on bge-small too.** `pytest -m llm` uses the same pinning, so only the scenarios (53/53 earlier) currently test the model your chats use.

**Why not remote everywhere:**
- Lessons 5–7 and the default test run should stay local: they work offline, need no key, give the same results every run, and you can watch every step.
- If everything were remote, you'd need a key and network for every test run. The provider could also change the model and move scores without anyone noticing.
- Mixing models is safe: each model's vectors live in their own property and index.

**What I'd change:**
1. **Recommend remote for the companion.** It already needs an LLM endpoint, and DeepInfra serves Qwen from the same endpoint. So `.env.example` and the README would present `EMBED_BASE_URL` as the normal setup, with local as the offline fallback.
2. **Make the tests model-aware.**
   - Tests that check a threshold would read it from the active model's thresholds instead of a typed number.
   - The few tests that really are about bge-small (its cross-encoder labels, its calibration pairs) would be skipped on the remote model, with a reason.
   - The Bob/Robert test would give "Bob" as an alias, the way the extractor does.
   - Then `TEST_REMOTE_EMBEDDINGS=1 pytest` should pass completely on Qwen.
3. **Add a documented "release check":** the full suite, the LLM evals and the scenarios, all on the remote model. Default `pytest` stays local and fast.

Nothing is changed or committed yet, including last turn's review edits. Should I do both 1 and 2 (with 3 in the docs), or only make the tests model-aware?
Yes, do both

## LLM settings (lessons 5 and 7–19)

Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint with tool calling works (OpenAI, DeepInfra, OpenRouter,
Ollama, LM Studio, vLLM...). Set in `.env`:

| Key | |
|---|---|
| `LLM_BASE_URL` | e.g. `https://api.openai.com/v1`, `http://localhost:11434/v1` |
| `LLM_MODEL` | chat model name |
| `LLM_API_KEY` | key (any value for local servers) |
| `LLM_EXTRACTION_MODEL` | optional, model for memory extraction (defaults to `LLM_MODEL`) |
| `LLM_TEMPERATURE` | chat temperature |
| `COMPANION_USER`, `COMPANION_NAME` | default user and companion names |

Embeddings run locally by default (`BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` via fastembed), no key needed.
Lessons 5–7 and the test suite always use that local model. The companion can use a remote
model instead (Lesson 19 has the full table of what runs where).
Lesson 19 switches the companion to a remote model with three more keys:

| Key | |
|---|---|
| `EMBED_BASE_URL` | an OpenAI-compatible `/embeddings` endpoint; empty = local bge-small |
| `EMBED_MODEL` | e.g. `Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-8B`; needs a measured profile in `companion/embeddings.py` |
| `EMBED_API_KEY` | optional, defaults to `LLM_API_KEY` |

After switching, run `.venv/bin/python -m companion.reembed`. The tests always use the local
model. The reranker that labels unrelated recall matches also runs locally (`RERANK_MODEL`,
default `Xenova/ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2`, Lesson 18; not used when the embedding profile sets
`weak_below`, Lesson 19). Local models are downloaded once and loaded once per process.

## Tests and evals

Every lesson has tests in [`tests/`](tests), named after it (`test_05_vectors_and_graphrag.py`).

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest                    # unit + database tests: seconds, free (default)
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -m "not db and not llm"   # unit tests only, no Neo4j needed
.venv/bin/python -m pytest -m llm             # LLM evals: real calls, cost money
EVAL_TRIALS=3 .venv/bin/python -m pytest -m llm tests/test_11_extraction_evals.py   # pass rates
```

A `-m` on the command line *replaces* the default `-m "not llm"` in `pytest.ini`, so spell
out `and not llm` when you add your own filter. Database tests never leave data behind: writes run in rolled-back transactions, and memory
tests use their own `pytest` user. A test for a lesson you haven't done yet is skipped with a
reason. [Lesson 0](lessons/00-setup.md#test-it) explains the three kinds of test, and each
lesson ends with a *Test it* section on what its tests teach.

### Where each model runs, after this lesson

| What | Model | Runs | Why there |
|---|---|---|---|
| Your chats (CLI and web UI) | Qwen3-Embedding-8B, if `EMBED_BASE_URL` is set | remote API | best separation of related and unrelated memories |
| The same, with `EMBED_BASE_URL` empty | bge-small | fastembed, CPU | no key, offline, the course default |
| The test suite | bge-small | fastembed, CPU | offline, free, seconds; pins thresholds |
| Lessons 5–7 scripts | bge-small | fastembed, CPU | the learning examples need no account |
| "Loosely related" labels | the cross-encoder `ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2` | fastembed, CPU | only for models without a measured `weak_below` (bge-small) |
| Lesson 15 graph embeddings | FastRP | inside Neo4j (GDS) | they come from graph structure, not text |

content.text:
Yes, I'd switch. Speed isn't the main reason, though. The real gain is reproducibility.

**What's fragile now.** `requirements.txt` only gives minimum versions (`langgraph>=1.2`, `openai>=3.46`…). Someone setting up next spring gets whatever is newest that day, and LangChain, LangGraph and the OpenAI SDK all break things between major versions. Nothing records which versions the recorded outputs and the 197 passing tests came from.

**What uv gives you:**
- **A lockfile (`uv.lock`).** Every reader installs exactly the versions the course was tested with. Upgrading becomes a deliberate step: `uv lock --upgrade`, run the tests, commit.
- **A pinned Python version.** uv downloads the right Python itself, so there's no "my system Python is 3.9" problem.
- **One setup command and no activation.** `uv sync`, then `uv run pytest` and `uv run python -m companion`. `uv run` also re-syncs the environment if dependencies changed after a `git pull`.
- **Much faster installs.** fastembed pulls in onnxruntime and other large packages.

**The costs, which are small:**
- **One more tool to install.** It's a one-line install, and you already have uv 0.11 on this machine.
- **Editing 58 commands.** The docs have 58 `.venv/bin/python …` commands to change to `uv run python …`. That's mechanical. uv still creates `.venv`, so the old commands would keep working anyway.
- **A pip fallback.** Some readers won't want uv. I'd keep a `requirements.txt` generated from the lockfile (`uv export`), so `python -m venv` + `pip install -r requirements.txt` still installs the same tested versions.

**What I'd do:**
1. Add a `pyproject.toml` with the dependencies and the Python version, and generate `uv.lock` from what's installed now.
2. Regenerate `requirements.txt` from the lock, as the pip fallback.
3. Change the setup in Lesson 0 and the README to `uv sync`, with a short pip note, and change every command to `uv run …`.
4. Add a short "Concepts and design choices" row in Lesson 0: why a lockfile, and what pinning costs (you have to upgrade on purpose).
5. Run the test suite through `uv run`, check the links, then commit only when you say.

content.text:
Short answer: the part Entire needs to work is already committed, and everything private is already kept out. The three untracked files are optional, so it's your call.

**Already tracked:** the "Enable Entire" commit (`e539a76`, Nov 6) added two files:
- `.entire/settings.json`: Entire is on, and checkpoints are stored as git refs.
- `.entire/.gitignore`: keeps the machine-local parts out of git (`tmp/`, `metadata/`, `logs/`, `settings.local.json`, `redactors/local/`).

Entire's own setup help says that in an existing repo it "lists the configuration files to commit rather than committing them". So it expects these two to be in the repo. Session history doesn't go in your files at all; it's kept on separate git refs that are pushed alongside your commits.

**The three untracked files are agent instructions, not configuration:**
- `.entire/agent-guide.md` tells coding agents to look up code with `entire graph …` instead of grep.
- `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` contain one line each that points agents to that guide. `AGENTS.md` is read by Codex and others, `CLAUDE.md` by Claude Code.

Checkpoints, trails and search work whether or not these are committed. All they change is how agents working in this repo search the code.

**When to commit them:**
- **Commit** if you use agents on this repo from more than one place: another machine, Codex on GitHub (the two `codex/` branches suggest you do), or cloud sessions. Those agents only see the guide if it's in the repo.
- **Keep them local** if this tutorial is for readers. Anyone who clones it without the Entire CLI would have an agent told to run `entire graph` commands that don't exist on their machine. To keep them out of `git status` without changing the shared `.gitignore`, add the three paths to `.git/info/exclude`.

Since the repo is private and you use Codex on it, I'd commit them now. If you later share the tutorial, remove them from the shared repo or note in the README that they're optional.

Separately, Entire reports an update from 0.12.2 to 0.13.4. That's yours to run if you want it:

```bash
curl -fsSL https://entire.com/install.sh | bash
```

Should I commit and push the three files, or keep them local with `.git/info/exclude`?
what do you recommend?

I'd commit them.

1. **Your agents work in more places than this laptop.** The two `codex/` branches on GitHub mean Codex works on this repo, and it can only read the guide if it's committed. Committing keeps local agents and remote ones on the same instructions.
2. **The repo is private.** The only downside of committing, confusing readers who don't have the Entire CLI, doesn't apply yet.
3. **It's easy to undo.** If you publish the tutorial later, deleting three files, or adding one optional line to the README, takes a minute. Their content is just a pointer and a workflow guide, nothing sensitive.

One check before you decide: `CLAUDE.md` now loads that guide into every Claude Code session here. That includes the rule to use `entire graph` for every code lookup, which adds a step even for small edits. If you'd rather not have that rule in this repo at all, the right choice is to keep them local, not to commit them.

Should I commit and push the three files?
yes
